title: What are you doing?
goal: Use verbs for the first time — the ongoing form *-yor*, along with its negative and question forms.
bekal: form *geliyorum, gelmiyorum, geliyor musun* from the root *gel-*
build sentences in Turkish order: subject, time/place, object, verb
say what you're doing right now

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Kafede
dialogs.intro: Budi is waiting at the café by the sea. Emre, Fatma Hanım's son, comes in and sits down next to him.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.id: I'm studying Turkish. What are you doing?

lines.speaker: Emre:
lines.id: I'm waiting too. My friend is on his way.

lines.speaker: Emre:
lines.text: Türk kahvesi. Sen çay içmiyor musun?
lines.id: Turkish coffee. Don't you drink tea?
lines.literal: Turkish coffee-its. you tea not-drinking question-you?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: İçiyorum ama şimdi su istiyorum. Hava çok sıcak.
lines.id: I do, but right now I want water. It's really hot.
lines.literal: am-drinking-I but now water am-wanting-I. air very hot.

lines.speaker: Emre:
lines.id: True. So where are you staying?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Sizin evde kalıyorum! Annen ev sahibim.
lines.id: I'm staying at your place! Your mother is my landlady.
lines.literal: your house-at am-staying-I! mother-your house owner-my.

lines.speaker: Emre:
lines.text: Ne? Sen Endonezyalı öğrenci misin? Annem hep senden bahsediyor!
lines.id: What? You're the Indonesian student? My mom talks about you all the time!
lines.literal: what? you Indonesian student question-you-are? mother-my always you-from is-talking!

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.id: I hope she says good things.

lines.speaker: Emre:
lines.text: Merak etme. Bu akşam ne yapıyorsun? Maç var.
lines.id: Don't worry. What are you doing this evening? There's a match.
lines.literal: worry don't-do. this evening what are-doing-you? match there-is.

notes: **The verb comes at the end of the sentence.** *Türkçe çalışıyorum* — "Turkish I-am-working". Throughout these twenty units that habit never changes: whatever you add to the sentence, the verb stays last.

**Geliyorum means "I'm in", not just "I'm coming".** When someone invites you and you agree, the answer is *geliyorum*. Turkish uses the ongoing form for near-future plans, much like English "I'm coming along".

**Bahsetmek requires -den.** "To talk about something" is *bir şeyden bahsetmek* — literally "to talk FROM something". Some Turkish verbs require a particular ending on their object, and the pair has to be learned together with the verb.
**Merak etme** is literally "don't do worry" — a negative command you'll learn properly in Unit 15. For now, just learn it as one phrase; you'll hear it every day in Turkey.

blocks.text: The dictionary form of a verb always ends in *-mek* or *-mak*: *gelmek* (to come), *almak* (to take). Drop that ending and you get the **root** — where every other ending attaches. *Gelmek* → *gel-*. *Almak* → *al-*.
To say something is going on, the recipe is: **root + linking vowel + yor + person ending**. The linking vowel is one of *ı, i, u, ü*, chosen by vowel harmony.

blocks.title: Yor never changes
items: Notice: whatever the verb's vowel, the piece **yor** is always written *yor* — never *yör* or *yar*. It's the only Turkish ending immune to vowel harmony, because it was originally a separate verb (*yorımak*, "to walk") that fused on many centuries ago.
That's also why the stress stops in front of it: *ge-LI-yo-rum*, not *ge-li-yo-RUM*.

blocks.text: If a root ends in *a* or *e*, that vowel **changes** to *ı/i/u/ü* — two vowels can't sit side by side:
Two verbs soften their consonant: *gitmek* → *gi**d**iyorum* (I'm going), *etmek* → *e**d**iyorum*. That's the entire list of Turkish "irregular" verbs — and the list ends here.
To make a negative, insert **-mı/-mi/-mu/-mü** between the root and *yor*. Note that the vowel has four forms, and the stress moves to the syllable before the insert.
To ask, use the particle *mu* from Unit 3 — and since *yor* always ends in *o*, the particle is **always mu**, no exceptions: *Geliyor musun?*, *Anlıyor musunuz?*, *Gelmiyor mu?*

blocks.title: One form, three jobs
items: *-yor* doesn't only describe what's happening this very second. It's also used for ongoing habits (*Bu sene Türkçe öğreniyorum* — this year I'm learning Turkish) and for near-future plans (*Yarın geliyorum* — I'm coming tomorrow).
That's why beginners can get by for a long time with this form alone. The other forms in Units 11 to 13 add precision; they don't replace it.

blocks.text: *Çalışmak* covers two things English keeps apart: "to work" and "to study hard". *Bir bankada çalışıyorum* = I work at a bank. *Türkçe çalışıyorum* = I'm studying Turkish. For "to go to school" Turkish uses *okumak* — the same word as "to read".

blocks.title: Unit 4 review
items: Cover the Turkish and rebuild it from memory: "This is my family." · "I have a younger brother." · "How old are you? (formal)" · "Ayşe's house is very nice." · "Whose photo is this?"

vocab.en: to read, to go to school
